sequences.source_document: Chakraborty et al. 2022, Solid Earth (XML text with PDF for figures)

steps.action: Took from the EEW literature the expectation that magnitude-estimate accuracy rises with the duration of P-wave data used.
steps.quote: The accuracy of such estimates has been shown to increase with the duration of data used to calculate them (Ziv, 2014).

steps.action: Posed the question of the optimum input duration for rapid magnitude characterisation from minimal P-wave data.
steps.quote: it becomes important to find an optimum duration for the input data

steps.action: Proposed a single-station deep-learning classifier sorting waveforms into noise, low-magnitude and high-magnitude (ML ≥ 5.0) classes.
steps.quote: we present a deep learning model to perform time series multiclass classification

steps.action: Tried magnitude 3 and 4 as alternative decision boundaries and reported similar accuracy, precision and recall; no numbers are given.
steps.quote: Magnitudes of 3 and 4 were also experimented with as decision boundaries

steps.action: Designed the test on STEAD: kept ML-scale traces with SNR ≥ 10 dB, split 60:10:30 into non-overlapping sets by event and station, and cut five P-wave durations (1, 3, 10, 20, 30 s).
steps.quote: we investigate the effect of using different lengths of data after the first P arrival (1, 3, 10, 20 and 30 s)

steps.action: Balanced the classes by augmenting high-magnitude events (shifted windows, polarity flips), undersampling low-magnitude and noise traces, and applying a 1:1:10 class weight chosen experimentally.
steps.quote: To tackle this imbalance problem, we apply resampling of the data (Krawczyk, 2016) as follows.

steps.action: Adopted the CNN plus bi-LSTM architecture from the authors' earlier abstract and trained it with Adam, cross-entropy loss, early stopping and learning-rate decay.
steps.quote: The model architecture (Chakraborty et al., 2021) consists of two sets of 1D convolution

steps.action: Fixed accuracy, precision and recall as the performance metrics for comparing durations.
steps.quote: we use the metrics listed below to evaluate the model performance

steps.action: Compared softmax probabilities for one waveform across durations (Fig. 5) and metrics across the five durations (Fig. 6a), finding no dependence on input length.
steps.quote: the predicted probabilities are different and show no dependence on the length of input data

steps.action: Retrained the 3 s model five times on the same data with untuned random seeds to measure initialisation randomness (Fig. 6b).
steps.quote: we also looked at the randomness in the performance when the model is trained on the same data five times

steps.action: Compared the spread across durations with the spread across retrainings and judged the two comparable.
steps.quote: the variation in the results caused by changing the length of data is comparable to the randomness in the results

steps.action: Read the confusion matrix and misclassification by magnitude for one 3 s model: errors concentrate near ML 5.0 and lean toward false high-magnitude alarms because of the class weights.
steps.quote: the misclassification of low-magnitude events as high-magnitude and vice versa is most pronounced at the decision boundary of 5.0

steps.action: Checked classification across hypocentral distance and SNR (Fig. 8) and inferred that the model is not simply mapping amplitude or SNR to magnitude.
steps.quote: there are instances of correct classification across a wide-range of hypocentral distances and signal-to-noise ratios

steps.action: Attributed the residual errors within 5.0 ± 0.5 to label uncertainty (inter-agency magnitude scatter of up to 0.5 units) rather than to the model.
steps.quote: even magnitudes of the same scale reported by different agencies can vary by as much as 0.5 magnitude units

steps.action: Proposed, without doing it, recasting the task as regression in a future version.
steps.quote: it might be helpful to treat this as a regression problem instead of classification

steps.action: Compared the overall accuracy (90.04–93.86 %) with the 93.67 % reported by Saad et al. (2020) using three stations.
steps.quote: which is comparable to the magnitude classification accuracy of 93.67 % achieved by Saad et al. (2020)

steps.action: Kept the claim that input length has no significant effect on performance and that accuracy reaches 93.86 %.
steps.quote: changing the length of the waveform (1, 3, 10, 20 or 30 s after P arrival) has no significant effect on the model performance

tree.answer: How input P-wave duration affects a deep-learning magnitude classifier
No; performance is measured on a held-out test set
Characterize a single-station classifier and the effect of input length
Implicit only: performance rises with length (traditional EEW) versus no effect
Not derived; no prediction or threshold is computed for either case
Set computationally: five durations, five retrainings, alternative boundaries
Duration spread falls within retraining spread; boundary, distance and SNR checks do not change the picture
Kept: no significant length effect; accuracy 90–94 %

end.claim: A single-station CNN plus bi-LSTM classifier separates noise, low-magnitude and high-magnitude (ML ≥ 5.0) STEAD waveforms with 90.04–93.86 % accuracy, and changing the input length from 1 to 30 s after P arrival changes performance no more than retraining randomness does.

decisive_move.sentence: Retraining the same model five times on the same data supplied the randomness baseline; without it, the spread across durations could not have been read as no significant effect.

gates.evidence: Action: the cited expectation that accuracy rises with data length (§1 ¶1) motivated the five-duration design (§2.1 ¶2), but no hypothesis is stated. Claim: performance could have risen with length, but the verdict is a visual judgement of comparability (§4 ¶1, Fig. 6), with no statistical test or threshold. Registration: nothing is reported as fixed before the data; the class weight was chosen experimentally (§2.1 ¶3).

imports.item: Deep learning for time series multiclass classification
1D convolution, dropout, max-pooling, bi-directional LSTM and softmax layers
Adam optimiser, categorical cross-entropy loss, early stopping
Resampling and class weighting for imbalanced data; data augmentation carried over from images
Accuracy, precision, recall and confusion-matrix evaluation

limits: No review file, open discussion or earlier version was supplied, so there is no review sequence, although the PDF records a public discussion. The verdict of no significant effect rests on a visual comparison: there is no statistical test, and the retraining baseline uses only five runs on the 3 s data, not on each duration. Inference: in Fig. 6b (p. 1726) iterations 4 and 5 show identical values, which may mean a duplicated run; the paper does not say. The retraining check is coded as a reproduction under codebook 3a, although it serves as the null baseline for the duration comparison. The decision-boundary checks (M3, M4) are reported without numbers. The class weight was chosen experimentally, and the text does not say on which split; inference: validation data. The comparison with Saad et al. (2020) uses different data and stations. Sub-claims at other statuses: the model learns frequency characteristics rather than amplitude or SNR (best_explanation, weakly supported by Fig. 8); errors near ML 5.0 reflect label uncertainty (best_explanation, argued from the literature, not tested). Composition is none_fits because the walk is a method characterization with a parameter sweep against a reproduction baseline, posed as a question before the capability; neither capability_first nor strong_inference describes it.

disagreements.target: Traditional EEW methods; Ziv (2014): accuracy of magnitude estimates increases with data duration
disagreements.support: Five input durations give a performance spread comparable to five retrainings on the same data, so for this classifier length shows no effect.
disagreements.quote: the variation in the results produced by changing the length of the data is no more than the inherent randomness in the trained models

disagreements.target: Saad et al. (2020), three-station magnitude classification
disagreements.support: A single-station model reaches 90.04–93.86 % accuracy against the 93.67 % reported for three stations, on different data.
disagreements.quote: Unlike Saad et al. (2020), who use data from three seismic stations to characterise different earthquake parameters

disagreements.target: Lomax et al. (2019), normalised single-station input
disagreements.support: None offered; the paper states it does not normalise and does not compare the two choices.
disagreements.quote: Unlike Lomax et al. (2019) we do not normalise the data.

alternatives_considered.chosen: Local magnitude 5.0 as the class boundary
alternatives_considered.reason: Boundary is arbitrary; can depend on the model's purpose and local geology

alternatives_considered.chosen: Three-component data from a single station
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Data from three stations (Saad et al., 2020)

alternatives_considered.chosen: Only traces with magnitude in the ml scale
alternatives_considered.reason: Consistency in magnitude; ml is the most common scale in the dataset

alternatives_considered.chosen: Resampling (augmentation and undersampling) plus a 1:1:10 class weight
alternatives_considered.alternatives: The original imbalanced distribution; other class weights (unspecified)
alternatives_considered.reason: Imbalance hinders classifiers and misleads accuracy evaluation; weight chosen experimentally

alternatives_considered.chosen: No instrument response removal and no normalisation
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Normalised data (Lomax et al., 2019); instrument response removal

alternatives_considered.reason: A single type would significantly reduce the training data and limit learning
Cites Bengio (2012) and Madhyastha and Jain (2019)
Regression would give the model more information about the exact magnitude (proposed for future work)
